blocks.body:
Quadratic reciprocity answers "is $a$ a square modulo $p$?". The next question is "is $a$ a cube modulo $p$?". For example, $2$ is a cube modulo $31$ (since $4^3 = 64 \equiv 2$) but not modulo $7$ (the only nonzero cubes mod $7$ are $1$ and $6$). Is there a rule?

The classical answer: for a prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the number $2$ is a cube modulo $p$ exactly when $p = x^2 + 27y^2$; and $31 = 2^2 + 27\cdot 1^2$. The natural home for such statements is the ring $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ of [[eisenstein-integers]], where Eisenstein proved the cubic reciprocity law in 1844. Along the way, cubic Gauss and Jacobi sums appear, and they encode the representation $4p = L^2 + 27M^2$ and the number of solutions of $x^3 + y^3 \equiv 1 \pmod p$.

blocks.title: Cubes modulo p
blocks.body:
If $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, then $\gcd(3, p - 1) = 1$ and the map $x \mapsto x^3$ is a bijection of $(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times$: every residue is a cube, and there is nothing to study.

If $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, let $g$ be a primitive root modulo $p$. Then $g^k$ is a cube exactly when $3 \mid k$, so exactly $(p-1)/3$ of the nonzero residues are cubes, and
$$a \text{ is a cube mod } p \iff a^{(p-1)/3} \equiv 1 \pmod p,$$
the cubic analogue of Euler's criterion: $a^{(p-1)/3} = g^{k(p-1)/3}$ equals $1$ exactly when $(p-1) \mid k(p-1)/3$, i.e. $3 \mid k$. For $p = 7$ the nonzero cubes are $\{1, 6\}$; for $p = 13$ they are $\{1, 5, 8, 12\}$. Since $-1 = (-1)^3$, the number $-1$ is always a cube.

blocks.title: Cubic character
blocks.body:
Let $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. A cubic character modulo $p$ is a nontrivial homomorphism $\chi: (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times \to \mathbb C^\times$ with $\chi^3 = 1$, extended by $\chi(0) = 0$. Its values are $1, \omega, \omega^2$, where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$.

There are exactly two: with a primitive root $g$, $\chi(g^k) = \omega^k$ and its conjugate $\bar\chi = \chi^2$, $\bar\chi(g^k) = \omega^{2k}$. For either one, $\chi(a) = 1$ if and only if $a$ is a nonzero cube, and $\chi(-1) = 1$.

blocks.title: The cubic residue symbol in Z[ω]
blocks.body:
To get a reciprocity law we need characters indexed by primes, so that "the character of $q$ evaluated at $p$" and "the character of $p$ evaluated at $q$" both make sense. In $\mathbb Z$ there is no natural choice between $\chi$ and $\bar\chi$, but in $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ there is.

Let $\pi$ be a prime of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ with $N(\pi) \ne 3$. The residue ring $\mathbb Z[\omega]/(\pi)$ is a field with $N(\pi)$ elements, and $N(\pi) \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ (it is $p \equiv 1$ or $q^2$ with $q \equiv 2 \pmod 3$). For $\alpha$ not divisible by $\pi$, the element $x = \alpha^{(N(\pi)-1)/3}$ satisfies $x^3 \equiv 1$, so $\pi$ divides $(x - 1)(x - \omega)(x - \omega^2)$ and hence one factor. The three values $1, \omega, \omega^2$ are distinct modulo $\pi$, because their differences are associates of $\lambda = 1 - \omega$, of norm $3$. So we may define the cubic residue symbol
$$\chi_\pi(\alpha) = \Bigl(\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\Bigr)_3 \in \{1, \omega, \omega^2\}, \qquad \chi_\pi(\alpha) \equiv \alpha^{(N(\pi)-1)/3} \pmod\pi,$$
and $\chi_\pi(\alpha) = 0$ if $\pi \mid \alpha$. It is multiplicative in $\alpha$, depends only on $\alpha$ modulo $\pi$, equals $1$ exactly when $\alpha$ is a nonzero cube modulo $\pi$, and satisfies $\chi_{\bar\pi}(\bar\alpha) = \overline{\chi_\pi(\alpha)}$.

When $N(\pi) = p$, the natural map $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z \to \mathbb Z[\omega]/(\pi)$ is an isomorphism, so restricting $\chi_\pi$ to integers gives a cubic character modulo $p$. The two cubic characters modulo $p$ are $\chi_\pi$ and $\chi_{\bar\pi} = \overline{\chi_\pi}$ on $\mathbb Z$.

blocks.title: Primary prime
blocks.body:
A prime $\pi = a + b\omega$ of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ with $N(\pi) \ne 3$ is primary if $\pi \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, that is, $a \equiv 2$ and $b \equiv 0 \pmod 3$.

Every such prime has exactly one primary associate. Reason: $\mathbb Z[\omega]/(3)$ has $9$ elements, of which $6$ are not divisible by $\lambda$; the six units are pairwise incongruent modulo $3$ (the difference of two distinct units has norm $1$, $3$ or $4$, never divisible by $N(3) = 9$), so they represent these $6$ classes, and as $u$ runs over the units, $u\pi$ runs over the same $6$ classes. Exactly one $u\pi$ is $\equiv 2$. Rational primes $q \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ are already primary. Primary is the cubic analogue of choosing the positive sign for an odd prime.

blocks.title: Cubic reciprocity (Eisenstein, 1844)
blocks.body:
Let $\pi_1, \pi_2$ be primary primes of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ with $N(\pi_1), N(\pi_2) \ne 3$ and $N(\pi_1) \ne N(\pi_2)$. Then
$$\chi_{\pi_1}(\pi_2) = \chi_{\pi_2}(\pi_1).$$
There are also supplementary laws for the units and for $\lambda = 1 - \omega$. (Proof omitted; the standard proof, in Ireland and Rosen, Ch. 9, uses the Gauss and Jacobi sums below.)

blocks.title: Cubic Gauss and Jacobi sums
blocks.body:
Let $\chi$ be a cubic character modulo $p$, $\zeta_p = e^{2\pi i/p}$, and define
$$g(\chi) = \sum_{t=0}^{p-1}\chi(t)\zeta_p^t, \qquad J(\chi, \chi) = \sum_{a=0}^{p-1}\chi(a)\chi(1 - a).$$
Then
$$g(\chi)^3 = p\,J(\chi,\chi), \qquad |J(\chi,\chi)| = \sqrt p.$$
Moreover $J(\chi,\chi) \in \mathbb Z[\omega]$, and if $\pi$ is primary with $N(\pi) = p$ then $J(\chi_\pi, \chi_\pi) = \pi$.

We prove the two displayed identities; the evaluation $J(\chi_\pi, \chi_\pi) = \pi$ is proved in Ireland and Rosen (Ch. 9) and is checked numerically below. That $J \in \mathbb Z[\omega]$ is clear, since $J$ is a sum of values of $\chi$.

Step 1: for characters $\chi, \psi$ with $\chi\psi$ nontrivial, $g(\chi)g(\psi) = J(\chi,\psi)\,g(\chi\psi)$, where $J(\chi, \psi) = \sum_a \chi(a)\psi(1 - a)$. Expand:
$$g(\chi)g(\psi) = \sum_{x, y}\chi(x)\psi(y)\zeta_p^{x+y} = \sum_t \zeta_p^t \sum_{x + y = t}\chi(x)\psi(y).$$
For $t \ne 0$ substitute $x = ta$, $y = t(1 - a)$: the inner sum is $(\chi\psi)(t)J(\chi,\psi)$. For $t = 0$ it is $\sum_x \chi(x)\psi(-x) = \psi(-1)\sum_x(\chi\psi)(x) = 0$. Hence $g(\chi)g(\psi) = J(\chi,\psi)\sum_t(\chi\psi)(t)\zeta_p^t = J(\chi,\psi)g(\chi\psi)$.

Step 2: take $\psi = \chi$. Since $\chi^2 = \bar\chi$ is nontrivial, $g(\chi)^2 = J(\chi,\chi)\,g(\bar\chi)$, so $g(\chi)^3 = J(\chi,\chi)\,g(\chi)g(\bar\chi)$.

Step 3: conjugating, $\overline{g(\chi)} = \sum_t\bar\chi(t)\zeta_p^{-t} = \bar\chi(-1)g(\bar\chi) = g(\bar\chi)$, using $\chi(-1) = 1$. So $g(\chi)g(\bar\chi) = |g(\chi)|^2 = p$ by the basic property of Gauss sums (see [[gauss-sums]]). This gives $g(\chi)^3 = pJ(\chi,\chi)$.

Step 4: taking absolute values, $p^{3/2} = |g(\chi)|^3 = p\,|J(\chi,\chi)|$, so $|J(\chi,\chi)| = \sqrt p$.

blocks.title: Everything for p = 7
blocks.body: Take $p = 7$ and the primitive root $3$, and let $\chi(3^k) = \omega^k$. Compute $\chi$, $J(\chi, \chi)$, and check the theorem.
blocks.solution:
The powers of $3$ modulo $7$ are $3^0 = 1$, $3^1 = 3$, $3^2 = 2$, $3^3 = 6$, $3^4 = 4$, $3^5 = 5$. So
$$\chi(1) = 1,\ \chi(3) = \omega,\ \chi(2) = \omega^2,\ \chi(6) = 1,\ \chi(4) = \omega,\ \chi(5) = \omega^2.$$
The cubes $1, 6$ get the value $1$, as they should.

In $J(\chi,\chi) = \sum_a\chi(a)\chi(1 - a)$ the terms $a = 0, 1$ vanish. The others:
$a = 2$: $\chi(2)\chi(6) = \omega^2$; $a = 3$: $\chi(3)\chi(5) = 1$; $a = 4$: $\chi(4)\chi(4) = \omega^2$; $a = 5$: $\chi(5)\chi(3) = 1$; $a = 6$: $\chi(6)\chi(2) = \omega^2$. So
$$J(\chi,\chi) = 2 + 3\omega^2 = 2 + 3(-1 - \omega) = -1 - 3\omega.$$
Its norm is $1 - 3 + 9 = 7$, so $|J| = \sqrt 7$. It is primary ($-1 \equiv 2$, $-3 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$), as the theorem predicts: this $\chi$ is $\chi_\pi$ for $\pi = -1 - 3\omega$. Numerically $g(\chi)^3 = 7(-1 - 3\omega)$.

Writing $J = a + b\omega$, the identity $4N(J) = (2a - b)^2 + 3b^2$ with $b = 3M$ gives $4p = L^2 + 27M^2$ with $L = 2a - b \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. Here $L = -2 + 3 = 1$, $M = -1$, and $28 = 1 + 27$.

blocks.title: When is 2 a cube?
blocks.body: Using cubic reciprocity, show that for a prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the number $2$ is a cube modulo $p$ if and only if $p = x^2 + 27y^2$ for some integers $x, y$.
blocks.solution:
Let $\pi = a + b\omega$ be primary with $N(\pi) = p$. Since $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z \cong \mathbb Z[\omega]/(\pi)$, $2$ is a cube modulo $p$ iff $\chi_\pi(2) = 1$. The number $2$ is a rational prime $\equiv 2 \pmod 3$, hence a primary prime of norm $4 \ne p$, so cubic reciprocity gives
$$\chi_\pi(2) = \chi_2(\pi) \equiv \pi^{(4-1)/3} = \pi \pmod 2.$$
So $\chi_\pi(2) = 1$ iff $\pi \equiv 1 \pmod 2$, i.e. $a$ odd and $b$ even. As $\pi$ is primary, $3 \mid b$; and $b$ even forces $a$ odd (else $2 \mid \pi$). So $2$ is a cube iff $b \equiv 0 \pmod 6$.

If $b = 6c$, then $p = a^2 - 6ac + 36c^2 = (a - 3c)^2 + 27c^2$. Conversely, if $p = x^2 + 27y^2$, replace $x$ by $-x$ if needed so that $x \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ (note $3 \nmid x$). Then $\pi_0 = x + 3y\sqrt{-3} = (x + 3y) + 6y\omega$ has norm $(x + 3y)^2 - 6y(x + 3y) + 36y^2 = x^2 + 27y^2 = p$, is primary, and has $b = 6y$. The primary primes of norm $p$ are $\pi$ and $\bar\pi = (a - b) - b\omega$, whose $b$-coordinates agree up to sign, so $b \equiv 0 \pmod 6$ for $\pi$ as well.

Check: $31 = 2^2 + 27$, and $2 \equiv 4^3 \pmod{31}$. The primary prime of norm $31$ is $-1 - 6\omega$, with $b = -6$. For $p = 7$, $\pi = -1 - 3\omega$ has $b$ odd, and indeed $2$ is not a cube modulo $7$.

blocks.title: Counting solutions of x³ + y³ ≡ 1
blocks.body: Let $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ and $4p = L^2 + 27M^2$ with $L \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. Show that the congruence $x^3 + y^3 \equiv 1 \pmod p$ has exactly $p - 2 + L$ solutions $(x, y)$, and deduce $\bigl|\#\text{solutions} - (p - 2)\bigr| \le 2\sqrt p$.
blocks.solution:
The number of $x$ with $x^3 \equiv u$ is $1 + \chi(u) + \bar\chi(u)$ for every $u$: it is $3$ for a nonzero cube, $0$ for a non-cube, and $1$ for $u = 0$. So the count is
$$N = \sum_{u + v = 1}\bigl(1 + \chi(u) + \bar\chi(u)\bigr)\bigl(1 + \chi(v) + \bar\chi(v)\bigr).$$
Expand into nine sums over $u + v = 1$. The term $1\cdot 1$ gives $p$. A term with exactly one character, such as $\sum_u\chi(u)$, is $0$. The remaining four are Jacobi sums: $J(\chi,\chi) + J(\bar\chi,\bar\chi) + J(\chi,\bar\chi) + J(\bar\chi,\chi)$.

For $J(\chi, \bar\chi) = \sum_{u \ne 0, 1}\chi\bigl(u/(1-u)\bigr)$, the map $u \mapsto u/(1 - u)$ is a bijection from $\{u \ne 0, 1\}$ onto $\{c \ne 0, -1\}$, so $J(\chi,\bar\chi) = \sum_{c \ne 0}\chi(c) - \chi(-1) = -1$. The same holds for $J(\bar\chi,\chi)$. Hence
$$N = p - 2 + 2\,\mathrm{Re}\,J(\chi,\chi).$$
With $J = a + b\omega$ primary (as in the theorem, taking $\chi = \chi_\pi$), $2\,\mathrm{Re}\,J = 2a - b = L$, the number with $L \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ in $4p = L^2 + 27M^2$. So $N = p - 2 + L$. Finally $L^2 \le 4p$ gives $|L| \le 2\sqrt p$.

For $p = 7$: $L = 1$ and $N = 6$; the solutions are $(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 4), (1, 0), (2, 0), (4, 0)$. For $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ cubing is a bijection, and $N = p$ exactly.

blocks.body:
- Conventions differ between books. The normalisation $\pi \equiv 2 \equiv -1 \pmod 3$ used here is sometimes relaxed to $\pi \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 3$. Since $-1$ is a cube, the sign does not affect cubic residue symbols, but it does affect identities such as $J(\chi_\pi,\chi_\pi) = \pi$.
- Which of the two characters is $\chi$ and which is $\bar\chi$ depends on choices (a primitive root, or $\pi$ versus $\bar\pi$). Statements that pick out one, like $J = \pi$, depend on this; statements like $\chi(a) = 1$ do not.
- Cubic reciprocity needs both primes primary and of different norms. For $\pi$ and $\bar\pi$ (same norm $p$) the law says nothing.
- For $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ there are no cubic characters modulo $p$; the corresponding primes of $\mathbb Z[\omega]$ are the inert $q$ with $N(q) = q^2$, and $\chi_q$ is trivial on ordinary integers coprime to $q$.

- The quadratic analogue is [[quadratic-residues]], with the quadratic Gauss sums of [[gauss-sums]]; quartic (biquadratic) reciprocity works the same way in the [[gaussian-integers]].
- Viewed as a function of the prime $\pi$, the Jacobi sum $J(\chi_\pi,\chi_\pi)$ is an example of a Hecke character of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, the kind of object whose $L$-functions are the [[hecke-l]] functions.
- A manuscript dated 30 September 2026, attributed to an OpenAI internal model, claims that every Dirichlet $L$-function is zero-free in $\mathrm{Re}\,s > \tfrac78$, using Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, cubic theta sums built from these characters, and a Mellin continuation; it was reported as Lean-verified. An October 2026 preprint (arXiv 2610.12234) claims to widen that half-plane by varying the parameters of the cubic theta argument. These are claims, not established results. A zero-free half-plane of this kind would go far beyond the classical [[zero-free-region]], which shrinks toward $\mathrm{Re}\,s = 1$ with the height; see [[quasi-rh]].

1. For $p = 19$ and the primitive root $2$, compute the cubic character $\chi(2^k) = \omega^k$, the Jacobi sum $J(\chi,\chi)$, and verify $4\cdot 19 = L^2 + 27M^2$.
2. Decide whether $2$ is a cube modulo $43$ and modulo $37$, and confirm by finding a cube root or showing there is none.
3. Show that $\chi(-1) = 1$ for every cubic character, and deduce that $g(\bar\chi) = \overline{g(\chi)}$.
4. Show that for $p \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ the congruence $x^3 + y^3 \equiv 1 \pmod p$ has exactly $p$ solutions.
